Asif: are you awake
Karthik: yeah, what happened
Asif: I need to tell you something and you can't laugh
Karthik: ok. not laughing
Asif: someone called and said I'd won a phone. I paid a "delivery fee" through a link
Asif: then they asked for more for "customs". I paid that too, two days ago
Asif: I told nobody. I thought you'd all say I'm stupid
Karthik: they run this on hundreds of people, Asif. Have you told your bank?
Asif: no. Every day I waited felt worse. They keep messaging me for more
Karthik: stop replying. Call the bank's helpline now and report it on the cyber crime portal. I'll sit next to you while you do it
Asif: ok. give me ten minutes to find the card

qa.q: What did the caller say Asif had won?
qa.a: The caller said Asif had won a phone.

qa.q: Why did Asif wait two days before telling anyone?
qa.a: Asif feared people would say Asif was stupid, and the messages show that waiting only made each day feel worse.

qa.q: What would you advise Asif to do right now?
qa.a: Stop replying to the scammers, call the bank's helpline, and report it on the cyber crime portal, ideally with Karthik sitting next to Asif. 🤍

qa.q: How does Karthik see what happened to Asif?
qa.a: Karthik sees it as something that happens to hundreds of people, not proof of stupidity, and offers to sit next to Asif while the calls are made.

grounding: Asif hides a scam out of fear of mockery, the silence lets it grow, and speaking up early leads to reporting.

Leela's phone buzzed with a forwarded poster from Chetan: "guaranteed profit every week", with a screenshot of someone's payout. Underneath he had typed, "My cousin's already in, this is real. Join before Friday!"

Leela felt her stomach tighten. Chetan was the friend who had lent her his notes all semester, and he meant well. She didn't send a joke back. She searched the scheme's name, found no sign of who ran it and a long page of complaints, then called him instead of texting.

"I looked it up, Chetan, and I can't find who's behind it. Could you ask your cousin where the money actually goes?"

He was quiet. "I just don't want to miss out."

"I know. I'm not joining, but come for chai tomorrow?"

"...Fine. Bring the notes back."

qa.q: Who had forwarded the poster to Leela?
qa.a: Chetan forwarded the poster, which promised "guaranteed profit every week".

qa.q: What does Chetan mean when he says "I just don't want to miss out"?
qa.a: Chetan is afraid of losing a chance that his cousin seems to be enjoying, so he believes in the scheme because he does not want to be left behind.

qa.q: What could Leela try next if Chetan keeps forwarding the scheme?
qa.a: Leela could keep asking calm questions about who runs it and where the money goes, share what she found, and keep meeting him while still refusing to join.

qa.q: How might Leela see Chetan's forwarded poster?
qa.a: Leela sees Chetan as a friend who means well, but the poster worries her, since she found no sign of who ran the scheme and a long page of complaints.

grounding: A friend forwards a guaranteed-profit scheme he believes in, and Leela checks the source, questions calmly and keeps the friendship while refusing.

On the bus home from the kasba, Harish kept rereading the number that had called about his "electricity bill". The caller had said the connection would be cut tonight and talked him into installing a screen-sharing app. Within minutes his account was lighter.

His jaw was tight. He had a plan: message the number as a buyer, set a meeting near the bus stand, and catch the man himself.

At the tea stall he told Ojas everything. Ojas shook their head. "Give the number, the screenshots and the bank message to the cyber cell. If you go alone you could lose more, or get hurt."

Then a new message arrived: "We recover lost money. Pay a small fee first." Harish's thumb hovered. Ojas took one look and said, "That's the same trick again."

Harish breathed out and handed over the phone.

qa.q: Where did Harish tell Ojas everything?
qa.a: Harish told Ojas everything at the tea stall.

qa.q: What was Harish feeling and wanting after the call?
qa.a: Harish was furious, with his jaw tight, and he wanted to catch the man himself by pretending to be a buyer.

qa.q: What was the wise step Ojas suggested, and why?
qa.a: Ojas suggested giving the number, screenshots and bank message to the cyber cell, because chasing the man alone could mean losing more or getting hurt.

qa.q: How does Ojas see the "recover lost money" message?
qa.a: Ojas sees it as the same trick again, a fee-first offer aimed at someone who is angry and wants the money back. 🤍

grounding: Harish is furious and wants to trap the fraudster himself, but hands his evidence to the cyber cell instead of chasing alone.

passage:
So I'm Hemant, and yes, I fell for a fake job offer that wanted a "registration fee". I found out when the company stopped answering.

When I told my father, Omkar, he shouted, "How could you fall for this?" I went hot all over. I already felt stupid, and now it felt like he was agreeing. I had a line ready about the lottery call he once believed. I didn't say it.

Because I noticed his hands were shaking. He wasn't only angry, he was scared about the money and about me.

So I said, "Papa, I'm scared too. Will you come with me to the bank and the cyber cell? And after that I'll show you the signs on your phone, the fee and the hurry."

He went quiet, then said, "Get your shoes."

qa.q: What did the fake job offer ask Hemant to pay?
qa.a: It wanted a "registration fee".

qa.q: What was Hemant feeling when Omkar shouted, and what did Hemant notice that changed the reply?
qa.a: Hemant felt hot and hurt, then noticed Omkar's hands were shaking, which showed that Omkar was scared about the money and about Hemant, not only angry.

qa.q: What might Hemant do if his father starts blaming him again later?
qa.a: Hemant could name the fear he sees, keep asking for help with the next steps, and keep offering to teach Omkar the scam signs instead of blaming back.

qa.q: What is it like for Omkar in that moment?
qa.a: Omkar is frightened for Hemant and about the money, and shouting is how the fear comes out, so calm help and a task like going to the bank gives Omkar something to do.

grounding: A parent scolds the young person who was scammed, who feels doubly hurt, hears the fear behind it and asks for help while offering to teach scam signs.

In the college library's computer corner, Samir paused a video. A finance influencer leaned on a red sports car and said his course had changed his life. Samir's thumb hovered over the "Enrol now" button. He could almost feel the leather seat.

Francis, from the economics society, leaned over. "How does he actually earn? From trading, or from selling the course?"

Samir blinked. He hadn't asked that.

They looked. No registration number was mentioned anywhere. The comments were switched off. The only proof of results was a set of screenshots the influencer had posted himself.

Samir closed the payment page and let out a slow breath. "I wanted the car more than I wanted the answer," he said.

Francis grinned. "Ask him for a track record next time."

qa.q: Where was Samir when he watched the video?
qa.a: Samir was in the college library's computer corner.

qa.q: What was Samir feeling as his thumb hovered over the "Enrol now" button?
qa.a: Samir felt drawn in by the sports car and the promise of a changed life, almost feeling the leather seat, and he had not yet asked how the money was made.

qa.q: What small steps did Samir and Francis take to check the influencer?
qa.a: They asked how the influencer actually earns, looked for a registration number and a track record, and found only screenshots the influencer posted himself.

qa.q: How might Francis see Samir's reaction to the video?
qa.a: Francis, from the economics society, seems to understand the pull of the cars and keeps the tone friendly, treating the missing evidence as a question to ask rather than a reason to mock Samir.

grounding: A finance influencer's luxury cars draw Samir in until he asks how the influencer earns and checks registration and track record.

passage:
The village cyber shop had one working fan, and Pranav sat under it staring at a group message: a countdown clock, "ONLY 5 SEATS LEFT", and screenshots of strangers' profits. The clock had eleven minutes on it. His savings from the harvest season were in the phone wallet.

His heart was racing. Everyone in the group seemed to be saying "joined!"

His sister Vidya, home for the weekend, glanced at the screen. "Why is the timer red?"

"So I don't miss it."

"Or so you don't think." She scrolled up. "Where are the risks written? Everything here is screenshots."

Pranav looked at the clock again. Then he closed the group, put the phone face down, and said, "Let's read the fine print first, didi."

qa.q: How many seats did the message say were left?
qa.a: The message said "ONLY 5 SEATS LEFT".

qa.q: Why was Pranav's heart racing?
qa.a: The countdown clock and the messages saying "joined!" made Pranav fear he would miss out, so he felt pushed to hurry with his harvest savings.

qa.q: What would you advise Pranav to do before putting money in?
qa.a: Slow down, read the risks in writing, treat the countdown as a sales tool, and only ever use money he could afford to lose.

qa.q: How does Vidya see the red timer differently from Pranav?
qa.a: Vidya sees the timer as pressure meant to stop people thinking, while Pranav sees it as a real deadline, which is why she asks where the risks are written.

grounding: Countdown timers, limited seats and profit screenshots pressure Pranav to hurry until his sister helps him slow down and look for the risks.

passage:
Monday. Wasim showed the group his phone: the money he'd put on a friend's hot tip had doubled in three weeks. Everyone cheered. Suraj clapped a beat late. That night he kept thinking he'd been saving carefully for two years and had gone nowhere. He opened a message to his cousin to ask about a loan, then left it unsent.

Friday. Suraj read a long thread about people who lost money on tips, most of whom never posted. He asked Wasim over chai, "Did you ever take a tip that failed?" Wasim rubbed his neck. "Yes. Twice. I don't talk about those."

The following Thursday. Suraj finished a free beginner's guide that explained index funds, spreading money across many things, and how time helps. He deleted the unsent message to his cousin and set a small monthly amount aside instead.

qa.q: How long did it take for Wasim's money to double?
qa.a: Wasim's money had doubled in three weeks.

qa.q: What was Suraj feeling on Monday night, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Suraj felt envious and left behind, since he clapped a beat late and kept thinking he had saved carefully for two years and gone nowhere.

qa.q: What went right in Suraj's choices between Monday and Thursday?
qa.a: He did not borrow, he learned that losers rarely post, and he read about index funds, spreading money out and time before setting aside a small amount.

qa.q: Why might Wasim not mention his failed tips to the group?
qa.a: Wasim rubs his neck and says he doesn't talk about those, which suggests the losses feel embarrassing and the wins are the part that gets shared.

grounding: Suraj envies Wasim's doubled money, nearly borrows to chase it, then learns that survivor stories hide the losers and studies the basics.

"Vidya, that's the fifth time you've looked at your phone since we sat down."

"Just checking. It dropped again. Look."

"You said you'd stop at lunch."

"I know. It's down a little and if I put a bit more in now I'll get it back when it climbs."

"Hm. And how was your mood this morning when it was green?"

"Fine. Great, actually."

"And now?"

Vidya stared at the red number. "Awful. My tea's gone cold and I haven't heard one word you said."

"That sounds less like planning and more like a slot machine, no?"

She was silent. Then she pressed and held the app icon. "Okay, Raghav. Notifications off, and I only look once at night. No more money in to fix it."

qa.q: How many times had Vidya looked at her phone since they sat down?
qa.a: Vidya had looked at her phone five times since they sat down.

qa.q: What was Vidya feeling when she said "Awful"?
qa.a: Vidya felt low because the red number had taken over her mood, so she stopped hearing Raghav and let her tea go cold.

qa.q: What limits does Vidya set, and why do they help?
qa.a: She turns off notifications, looks only once at night and adds no more money to fix a loss, which breaks the loop of checking and doubling down.

qa.q: How might Raghav feel watching Vidya check the app?
qa.a: Raghav probably feels worried and a little ignored, but keeps the questions gentle so Vidya can notice the pattern herself.

grounding: Vidya checks a trading app constantly and her mood follows the chart until she sees it as a gambling loop and sets limits.

passage:
Sit, Parveen, let me tell you something from when I was twenty-one. I'm Imran, and back then I was the commerce student in our friend group.

One evening four friends came to me. "You understand markets. Put our money together and invest it for us." I felt so flattered, like I was finally somebody. And underneath I felt a weight, because I knew I only understood a little from a few classes.

I didn't take it. I said, "I know less than you think. I won't hold your money, and I can't promise any returns. If you want to learn, I'll study with you."

One friend sulked for a month. But none of us lost anything, and he came back.

qa.q: How old was Imran when the friends asked to have their money invested?
qa.a: Imran was twenty-one.

qa.q: What two feelings did Imran have when his friends asked?
qa.a: Imran felt flattered, as if finally somebody, and also burdened by a weight because he knew he understood only a little.

qa.q: What would you say to a young person asked to invest friends' money?
qa.a: Be honest about your limits, do not hold others' money or promise returns, and offer to study together or point them to a qualified adviser.

qa.q: How did the friends see Imran's refusal at first?
qa.a: One friend sulked for a month, probably feeling turned down after showing trust, but he came back once nothing was lost.

grounding: Friends want Imran to pool their money because he understands markets, and he admits his limits and refuses to hold money or promise returns.

passage:
Tuesday night

Today most of my savings vanished. A stranger in a group said "sure thing, this stock will jump", and I put nearly everything in. It fell by evening. I keep opening the app as if it will take it back.

I feel so foolish. Two years of tuition money, gone in one afternoon 😔

Imran bhai called and said he had another "sure thing" that could win it all back by Friday. I said no. My hands were sweating while I said it, but I said no.

Okay. Rules for tomorrow: no app, no groups. Write down what I'll remember: I trusted a stranger's confidence instead of proof, and I bet what I couldn't lose.

Slowly, then. Tomorrow I'll put the first small amount back into my account.

Usha

qa.q: Who called Usha with another "sure thing"?
qa.a: Imran bhai called with another "sure thing" that could win the money back by Friday.

qa.q: Why does Usha feel foolish tonight?
qa.a: Usha put nearly everything into a stranger's tip and watched it fall, and the diary says it was two years of tuition money gone in one afternoon.

qa.q: What did Usha do that will help her recover, and what could she add?
qa.a: Usha refused another risky bet, decided to stay off the app and groups, and wrote down the lesson; talking to a trusted adult about rebuilding slowly could also help.

qa.q: How might Imran bhai see Usha's refusal?
qa.a: Imran bhai may think he is offering help with a quick way to win it back, so Usha's no could seem cautious to him, but it stops a second loss.

grounding: Usha loses most of the savings on a tip, feels foolish, refuses another risky bet, writes the lesson and plans to rebuild slowly.
